newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS- NOV 21.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:
KATHIMERINI

--The government is thoroughly reviewing its proposals on taxation of state titles and derivatives following the flurry of reaction to their announcement on Tuesday. Sources say Prime Minister Costas Simitis wants a thorough re-examination of all details involved in the proposed taxes to avert any questioning of government credibility and put an end to the fuzziness that caused uncertainty in the interbank market on Tuesday.
--Simitis also gave the go-ahead for the government economic team to begin a round of contacts with banks and the Bank of Greece on the details of how to tax derivatives and bonds.
--The finance ministry is concerned with whether the forecast gains from the new taxes will be forthcoming.

--Brokerage firms must supply general information on their transactions within 48 hours to the three international houses conducting checks, while the clearing house announces five firms have not met the requirements and may be barred from trading today.
IMERISIA

--The business world greets the government's taxation proposals with a storm of protest: rather than restricting state spending, the Simitis is restricting competitiveness and, subsequently, economic growth, they say.

--A meeting last night between trade unionists aligned to ruling party PASOK saw intense disagreements over the government's economic choices. A new poll commissioned by the party, however, shows the majority of Greeks supporting harsh measures if they are deemed to be fair.

--The construction of the road project which will change the transit map of Attica and is the biggest road project in Greece gets under way. Parliament last night approved the contract for the Elefsina-Spata airport-Western region road - to be built almost exclusively by Greek firms, creating 10,000 jobs over the five-year construction period.
--Greece's telecommunications organisation OTE announces an agressive 100 billion drachma investment drive targeting the Balkans and Eastern Europe.

--Thirty-six public sector organisations are to become limited liability companies by the end of the year: implementation of the new law has been difficult as administrations of public utilities and organisations (DEKO) resist the change.
KERDOS
--Federation of Greek Industries (SEB) President Jason Stratos calls for radical, structural changes and fears that the government's new measures will work as disincentives to prospective investors.
--The new three-year fixed-rate bonds will be up for auction in a favourable climate tomorrow, following the finance ministry's clarification of the taxation of the interbank market.
--The finance ministry finds a new formula calming bankers anbd the market following the negative reaction to the proposal for taxation on interbank deposits.
--OTE shareholders to receive a dividend of 155-160 drachmas for 1996, up from 130 drachmas in 1995.
--Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis sets to house cleaning the public sector's banking accounts.
EXPRESS

--The new taxes will not meet the targets of the convergence programme, SEB President Jason Stratos says. "The policy announced is ineffective and the measures simply the imposition of new taxes," he says.
NAFTEMBORIKI

--Deposits and loans in foreign exchange will remain tax-free, according to all indications, as the interbank market calms following the clarification from the deputy finance minister on the government's taxation proposal.

--Investments by public utlities and organisations (DEKO) are expected to total 1.3 trillion drachmas, a 20 percent increase in relation to 1996. The increase will be marked mainly in the energy, power, and transport sectors and a large part will be co-financed by EU funds. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
